turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on back, Mr. Hale. I'm gonna peel this dressing off so Dr. Ellison can actually see the incision. Appendectomy was ten days ago, yeah?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Yeah. Last Tuesday? Or, wait, Wednesday. I don't know. Ten days sounds right.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ten days, that's right. I drove him home. I'm June, I stay days while he gets back on his feet.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ellison. Thanks for waiting. What's going on with the wound?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's red. And there's, um, gunk coming out onto the bandage. I don't know, doctor, it just looks bad.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did that redness start?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The tape yanks my skin off every time we change it. Hurts like crazy.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yeah, the tape is miserable. I do still need when the redness showed up. Yesterday? Before that?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple days. Maybe three. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I saw pink on Thursday, so four days, and it got a lot redder yesterday.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright, so about three or four days, we won't force an exact day. Drainage too? What color?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yellow. Sticky. Not pouring out, just sitting on the gauze.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Okay, dressing's coming off. Might pull.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yeah. Sorry.

[SEG0015] person_1 (NURSE): Right lower incision, about two inches. Edges mostly together. Red maybe an inch all the way around, warm to the touch, and a little yellow drainage at the lower end. It's not gaping open.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any odor from it?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): That was a pretty soft answer. Does it actually smell?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I don't know.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then I won't write down a smell. Fever at all?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night I got hot. And kind of achy. I don't know if it was a real fever.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I took it around nine. It read a hundred and one point two.
[SEG0023] person_1 (NURSE): Here he's ninety-nine point one, pulse ninety-two, pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-six, sat ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I've been eating toast. That's been fine, I guess.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shaking chills with the fever?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Her car's been making this awful noise, that's why we were late. I've just been living in the recliner.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Different question got answered there. Any chills, where you were shaking?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. No, I don't think so.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Burning when you pee?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The incision itches under the tape. That's what makes me nuts.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the bladder alone, then. What medicines did they send you home with? Antibiotics?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): The pink capsules. I took them five days... or was it seven? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Cephalexin. He's been on it. I'm not sure about the midday one, he sleeps right through it.
[SEG0035] person_1 (NURSE): Discharge med rec says cephalexin five hundred milligrams by mouth four times a day.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Huh. That's not our bottle. I read it this morning, two hundred fifty milligrams, four times a day. Same drug.

[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me play that back. The chart says five hundred four times a day, the bottle at home says two fifty four times a day, you're unsure if it was a five-day or a seven-day course, and the midday dose may have been skipped.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. There might be two pills left. Or I'm done. I don't know.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Either way, no more cephalexin. We'll change it. What else was prescribed?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, six hundred milligrams. I stopped that three days ago. Stomach was burning.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stopped the ibuprofen three days ago because your stomach burned. Was there a narcotic too?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Oxycodone. I never took it. Not once. Those make me loopy.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the oxycodone was never started. Any allergies to medications?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hospital band said no known allergies. He hasn't mentioned a reaction to me.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I remember.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): No known allergies. I'm going to look at the incision myself.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Same as the nurse said. Warm, red, a little yellow drainage, and it's still mostly closed. This is most in keeping with a superficial wound infection.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): A deep abscess is unlikely while it's holding together, but the exam doesn't fully rule that out. We'll swab the drainage.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): I can grab the culture swab before I redress it.

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please do, send a wound culture. And I'm switching the antibiotic to amoxicillin-clavulanate, eight hundred seventy-five milligrams, one tablet by mouth twice a day for seven days, for this wound infection.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice a day I can probably remember. I think.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put an alarm on my phone so we're not guessing.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Keep it clean and dry. Showers are okay if you pat it dry, no baths. Dry gauze once a day.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it gets bad tonight? I don't know what counts as bad, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads, the drainage increases, or the fever comes back, call or go to the ER. Otherwise I want you back here in two days to recheck it.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two days works. I'll get him here.
[SEG0058] person_1 (NURSE): I'll lay a dry dressing on once that swab is collected.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the new one gonna burn my stomach like the ibuprofen did? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): It can. Take it with food. And don't restart the ibuprofen.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. No more pink capsules. Two days.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's the plan. Stop the cephalexin, start the new antibiotic today, culture goes to the lab, and I'll see you in two days.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
